correctness.rationale: Over an algebraic closure in characteristic ≠2, an odd theta characteristic remains odd after translation by a≠0 precisely when its quadratic refinement vanishes on a; the resulting pairs give Steiner membership. Independently I used even subsets of eight letters modulo complement: q(S)=|S|/2 mod 2 has 36 zeros, and its polarization is parity of intersection, with radical removed by the complement quotient. The 28 nonsingular classes are the pairs and label the odd refinements q+ω(v,−); the 63 nonzero classes label complexes. The resulting integer incidence has row degree 27, column degree 12 and BB^t=16I+11J, yielding a connected 91-vertex, 756-edge graph and cycle rank 666. The exact Laplacian characteristic polynomial and integer cofactor agree; the latter factors as 2^124·3^36·7^26·11^27. Direct Smith reduction of the cofactor returns 1×28,2×6,4×20,12×9,132,924×20,1848×6. This verifies the full integer invariant, not only mod-prime ranks. The source's minimum-valuation pivot argument uses invertible operations modulo the stated prime powers, with all final pivot valuations below precision.
residual_risks: The result is geometric and specifically for this theta-theoretic design, not all abstract 2-(28,12,11) designs, nor a Frobenius-module statement. The Néron-component application is conditional on the prescribed split regular unit-thickness dual graph.

value.rationale: The natural theta-to-Steiner incidence gives a characteristic-independent geometric graph in the stated range. Its complete graph Jacobian records higher 2-adic torsion and the combined exponent 1848, neither read from the tree number nor from the known rectangular Steiner-sum group. The exact quotient is useful for integral chip-firing on this design or as the component group for a suitable split regular unit-thickness smoothing of a stable curve with that graph.
residual_risks: Finiteness and computation alone do not provide an equivariant refinement or a canonical degeneration of the given quartic; neither is claimed.
